title: Why is four thirds more than one?
description: Four thirds is compared with one whole unit by adding thirds. The board shows three thirds filling the unit and one more third going past it. Keeko doubts the result because a third looks like a small piece.
teaching_notes: One idea: three thirds make one whole, so one more third takes the total past one. Watch for students who judge the total by the size of one small piece.

video_script.why: A learner explains why a fraction with one more part than the whole is greater than one.
video_script.substitution: the book's own fraction four thirds
video_script.anchor: a unit bar cut into three equal parts with one more third added after it
video_script.wrong_answer: four thirds is less than one, because a third is a small piece
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko judges the total by the size of one piece, not by how many pieces are added.
video_script.payoff_line: Four thirds is more than one

final_answer.value: 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 3/3 = 1; adding one more 1/3 gives more than 1 unit, so 4/3 > 1
final_answer.spoken: four thirds is more than one, because three thirds make one and one more third goes past it

video_script.fraction_reading: one third, three thirds, four thirds
maths_rules: 1 unit cut into 3 equal parts: each part is 1/3
4/3 is one more 1/3 than 3/3, so 4/3 is more than 1
check: on the number line the end of 4/3 lies one part past the mark 1
video_script.design: A unit bar of three thirds, then a fourth third drawn after the mark one. The number line from zero to two confirms it.

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Four thirds is more than one.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks four thirds is less than one, because a third is a small piece.
<bookmark mark='row'/>Lay the four thirds in a row. Small pieces still add up, and three of them already fill the unit.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The fourth third goes past one. How many pieces we add matters more than how small each is.
